articles.excerpt: Why Rust Web Development Sucked for Web Developers (Until Now) Let's be brutally honest for a moment: Rust web development has had an elitism problem. For the last five years, tech Twitter, Hacker New…
articles.body: Why Rust Web Development Sucked for Web Developers (Until Now) Let's be brutally honest for a moment: Rust web development has had an elitism problem. For the last five years, tech Twitter, Hacker News, and Reddit have proclaimed that Rust is the undisputed future of fast, memory-safe backend engineering. And on paper, it sounds irresistible: Zero garbage collection pauses 10x to 50x the throughput of Node.js and Python Microscopic 12MB RAM usage instead of Node’s 400MB bloat Zero random runtime crashes at 3:00 AM Naturally, thousands of backend engineers working in Node.js (Express/Fastify), Python (FastAPI/Django), and Go decided to give Rust a try.

articles.title: Choosing an Agent Memory Tool: Test Concurrent Corrections
articles.excerpt: Before choosing a long-term memory tool for an AI agent, test what happens when two sessions correct the same fact. Define the expected conflict policy, submit both changes from the same starting stat…
articles.body: Before choosing a long-term memory tool for an AI agent, test what happens when two sessions correct the same fact. Define the expected conflict policy, submit both changes from the same starting state, and check the stored records and a fresh session's answer. Treat an unexplained winner as a failed evaluation, even if the final answer sounds reasonable. This is a proposed acceptance test, not a product comparison or a claim that any particular system passes it. Run it with invented facts in a disposable project. Define what a correct outcome means Use a fictional project called Lantern. Its initial memory is: Lantern's review contact is Morgan. Record revision: R0. Session A will propose Casey as the new contact. Session B will propose Riley.

articles.title: Trying to break into the clinical trials space
articles.excerpt: Imagine someone has just been given a serious diagnosis. One of their options might be a clinical trial: a new drug or treatment regimen that isn't yet available in routine care. There's no shortage o…
articles.body: Imagine someone has just been given a serious diagnosis. One of their options might be a clinical trial: a new drug or treatment regimen that isn't yet available in routine care. There's no shortage of places to look. The largest open registry, ClinicalTrials.gov, is free and lists more than 600,000 studies from all over the world. So what's the problem? It's not that there's too little data. Quite the opposite: there's too much of it, and it's written for specialists. To figure out whether a trial is right for you, you have to read the inclusion and exclusion criteria and match them against your diagnosis, stage, previous treatment and a dozen other things. For someone without medical training, that means hours of comparing walls of text, and still a real chance of getting it wrong.

articles.excerpt: A nasty Chrome bug let hackers break into Android phones without a tap.
articles.body: TL;DR A security firm has found that hackers exploited a Chrome bug and a Qualcomm Adreno GPU driver flaw to infect Android phones that visited a booby-trapped website. The attack targeted Chrome versions 139 to 145 on Android and stole browser cookies, saved logins, browsing history, and Wi-Fi passwords. Both flaws had already been patched, so phones running up-to-date Chrome and security updates remained safe. Security researchers at Sekoia have detailed a mobile hacking campaign that went after Android and iPhone users through hijacked and fake websites. On Android, the attackers didn’t need victims to tap a link, install an app, or grant a permission. Opening an infected page in an outdated version of Chrome was enough.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 4, 2015: A rail-launched Super Strypi rocket carrying 13 baby satellites failed during its debut launch for the US Air Force
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force launched an experimental Super Strypi rail-launched rocket carrying 13 tiny satellites, but it failed just after liftoff from Hawaii.
articles.body: On Nov. 4, 2015, the United States Air Force planned to launch an experimental rocket for small satellites from the Pacific Missile Range Facility off Barking Sands, Kauai, Hawaii. The launch didn't according to plan . For this mission, the Air Force was testing out the Super Strypi rocket . The rocket used a rail to help with the liftoff. Super Strypi left the ground, but the rocket quickly spun out of control. When it crashed, it destroyed all of the tiny satellites riding aboard the rocket. The cause? Likely a problem with the first stage motor. The mission lost 13 tiny satellites known as cubesats. Cubesats are a popular option for space missions, because they are small and cheap, and they often operate in swarms.

articles.title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
articles.excerpt: Researchers say group may have been Kremlin-sponsored in search of diplomatic targets.
articles.body: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday. The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data.
